Dental Assistant Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A dental assistant resume has to prove two things in seconds. First, that you are certified for the work: CDA, state registration, and the X-ray credential that matches the practice. Second, that you keep the chair moving — patients seated, instruments ready, operatories turned over, charts current. A resume that lists duties without volumes reads like a job description. One that pairs each duty with a count reads like a clinician the practice can rely on.

This guide gives you a full annotated example from a general dentistry practice, a section-by-section breakdown, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works: what you did, at what volume, and with what result.

Quick answer: A dental assistant resume should include a summary naming your certification and setting; a chairside block with your patient volume, the procedures you assist, and radiography you take; a certifications block with CDA, X-ray, and CPR credentials; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day or instruments sterilized per week.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with certification and setting — CDA, state registration, X-ray credential, and the practice type and volume you handle.
  • Prove chairside speed with volumes: patients per day, X-ray sets per week, and operatory turnover time.
  • Name the procedures you actually assist: four-handed dentistry, digital radiography, impressions, sealants, sterilization.
  • Every experience bullet pairs a duty with a count: patients per day, instrument sets sterilized, or recall patients kept on schedule.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Dental Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a practice owner and you will not hear “passionate about helping people.” You will hear:

  • Certification, stated plainly. CDA from DANB, state registration where it applies, and the radiography credential, with the expanded-function permits that match the practice — sealants, coronal polishing. An uncertified applicant goes in a different pile.
  • Chairside volume. Patients per day, operatories covered, and the mix: general, restorative, cosmetic, hygiene. An assistant who seats 24 patients a day in a busy practice is a safer hire than one who lists duties without numbers.
  • Radiography competence. Digital X-ray sets per week, intraoral photos captured, and the retake rate. A clean first image saves the dentist a chair; a retake costs one.
  • Sterilization discipline. Autoclave cycles run, instrument sets processed, OSHA logs kept. Infection control is the part of the job a practice cannot afford to get wrong.
  • Software fluency. Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental, named exactly. Charts, scheduling, and recall live in that system, and a hire who needs weeks of training costs the practice a month.

If your resume reads like a duties list — all responsibilities, no volumes — it will lose to one that reads like a chairside record.

Dental Assistant Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is a complete example from a general dentistry practice. It’s fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: what you did, the volume, and the result.

AMARA OSEI, CDA, RDA
Phoenix, AZ · (602) 555-0183 · amara.osei@email.com

SUMMARY
Certified Dental Assistant (CDA, RDA) with 5 years in general dentistry, including 3 years at a 4-operatory practice seeing 120 patients a week. Seat and assist 24 patients a day across restorative, cosmetic, and hygiene cases; X-ray certified, 18 sets a week. Sealant and coronal polishing permitted; CPR current.

CERTIFICATIONS
Certified Dental Assistant (CDA), DANB · Registered Dental Assistant (RDA), Arizona · Radiation Health and Safety (RHS) · Coronal Polishing Permit · Sealant Placement Permit · CPR/BLS, current

SKILLS
Four-handed dentistry · Digital radiography · Intraoral photography · Alginate and digital impressions · Sealant placement · Coronal polishing · Fluoride application · Sterilization and autoclave · OSHA infection control · Dentrix · Eaglesoft · Patient intake · Treatment planning · Scheduling and recall · Insurance verification

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Dental Assistant — Desert Ridge Family Dentistry, Phoenix, AZ | 2021–Present

  • Seat and assist 24 patients a day across general, restorative, and cosmetic cases
  • Take 18 sets of digital X-rays a week and capture intraoral photos for every new-patient exam
  • Run sterilization for 30+ instrument sets a day, keeping operatory turnover under 10 minutes
  • Place sealants on 40+ patients a month and apply fluoride varnish across the hygiene schedule
  • Cut the no-show rate from 14% to 8% by tightening confirmations and filling cancelled slots from the waitlist
  • Keep Dentrix charts current with same-day charting across a 120-visit week

Dental Assistant — Bright Smile Orthodontics, Phoenix, AZ | 2019–2021

  • Assisted 20 orthodontic patients a day, preparing archwires, brackets, and elastics for adjustments
  • Took alginate and digital impressions for 15+ patients a week, with retakes under 1 in 20
  • Managed the sterilization room and tracked inventory, cutting supply waste by reordering on par levels
  • Trained 2 new assistants on four-handed technique, X-ray positioning, and Dentrix charting

Externship — Valley Dental Care, Phoenix, AZ | 2019 (12 weeks)

  • Completed a 12-week externship in general practice, assisting 10 patients a day across cleanings, fillings, and crowns
  • Took X-rays under supervision and logged 50+ radiographs for the certification portfolio

EDUCATION
Certificate in Dental Assisting — Phoenix College, 2019 · High School Diploma, 2017

Why it works: the summary leads with the certification and the two numbers practices check — patients per day and X-ray sets per week. Every bullet pairs a duty with a count, and the climb from externship to a 4-operatory practice shows progression.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: certification and setting first, then volumes

“CDA, RDA,” “4-operatory practice,” “24 patients a day,” “18 sets a week” — certification answers the eligibility question; volumes answer the competence question.

Experience: volumes and measures, not responsibilities

“Assisted the dentist” is a responsibility; “seat and assist 24 patients a day with turnover under 10 minutes” is proof of chairside effect. The strongest bullets show a number that moved because of work you did.

Certifications: exact letters, current status

List the credential exactly as it appears on the certificate, with the CDA and state registration up front. Hiring managers screen on these letters before reading experience — and expanded functions vary by state, so name only permits you actually hold.

Dental Assistant Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s language exactly: “four-handed dentistry” vs “chairside assisting” matters:

  • Chairside: four-handed dentistry, chairside assisting, instrument transfer, suction, tray setup, operatory turnover, patient seating
  • Radiography & imaging: digital radiography, dental X-rays, intraoral photography, panoramic X-rays, bitewing, periapical, DEXIS
  • Procedures: sealant placement, coronal polishing, fluoride application, alginate impressions, digital impressions, rubber dam placement
  • Safety: sterilization, autoclave, OSHA infection control, HIPAA, instrument processing
  • Systems: Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, electronic dental record, scheduling, recall, insurance verification
  • Credentials: CDA, RDA, DANB, radiation health and safety, RHS, CPR, BLS, coronal polishing

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Practices screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. Start from a clean template in Cvyon's template gallery, or the role page for dental assistants. Note the difference from the medical assistant role: medical assistants work under a physician across clinical and administrative tasks, while dental assistants work chairside with the dentist.

5 Mistakes That Cost Dental Assistants Interviews

  1. Hiding the certification. A resume that buries CDA, state registration, and the X-ray credential at the bottom forces the reader to hunt for the three lines that decide the pile. Put them in the summary and in their own block.
  2. Listing duties instead of volumes. “Assisted the dentist” is a job description; “24 patients a day with operatory turnover under 10 minutes” is chairside proof. Lead with volumes.
  3. Claiming an expanded function your state does not allow. Sealants and coronal polishing are permitted in some states and not others. State only permits you actually hold; practices verify them, and a claim that fails verification ends the application.
  4. No software named. Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental — a resume without a system reads as if charts were never done. Name the system and the years you used it.
  5. One generic resume for every practice. Tailor the summary and first bullets to the setting: volume and turnover speed for general dentistry, impression accuracy for orthodontics, calm and repetition for pediatric dentistry.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a dental assistant resume?

A summary naming your certification, state registration, and setting; a chairside block with patient volume, procedures assisted, and radiography taken; a certifications block with CDA, X-ray, and CPR credentials; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day or instruments sterilized per week.

How do I show chairside skills on a dental assistant resume?

Name the procedures and the volume: 24 patients a day in four-handed dentistry, 18 sets of digital X-rays a week, sealants on 40 patients a month. Add the turnover time you keep and the software you chart in, because speed and accuracy are what a hiring dentist reads first.

What certifications should a dental assistant list on a resume?

List the ones you actually hold: your CDA from DANB and state RDA first, then your radiography or X-ray certification, plus CPR or BLS and expanded-function permits such as coronal polishing or sealants where your state allows them. Never claim a credential you do not hold; practices verify before the first shift.

How long should a dental assistant resume be?

One page for most dental assistants, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a career across genuinely different settings, such as general dentistry, orthodontics, and oral surgery; even then keep the certification, the strongest volumes, and the X-ray credential on page one.

What is the difference between a dental assistant and a dental hygienist on a resume?

A dental assistant works chairside with the dentist, handing instruments, taking X-rays, and preparing materials. A dental hygienist cleans teeth, scales, and performs preventive care independently under the dentist's supervision. State the scope you actually held, and never claim cleanings or scalings you did not perform.

Do I need experience to get a dental assistant job?

Most practices hire new graduates, especially from a strong externship. An externship counts as experience if you name the setting, the weeks, the patients per day, and the radiographs you took. Lead with the externship and the certification, not with unrelated jobs.
